question: Why do you want to study Banking & Finance?
lookingFor: A genuine, specific motivation grounded in real exposure to money and markets, not a vague love of numbers.

bullets: Point to a concrete moment or experience that sparked the interest
Show you understand what the field actually involves day to day
Connect it to what you want from the course, not just the eventual salary
idealAnswer.modelAnswer: I started managing a small savings pot for my school's fundraising club in Year 11, and working out how to keep it safe but still growing was the first time economics stopped being abstract for me. That pulled me into reading about how banks actually price risk, which felt like the real machinery behind every decision I'd been making with our tiny fund. I want to study Banking & Finance because I want to understand that machinery properly, not just the headlines about it.

commonMistakes: Saying 'I'm good with numbers' with nothing else behind it
Talking only about wanting a high salary
Giving an answer that could apply to economics, business, or accounting equally
followUps: What was the first thing about finance that genuinely surprised you?

question: Why do you want to study Banking & Finance here specifically, rather than at another university?
lookingFor: Evidence of real research into the course structure, not generic praise or reputation-chasing.

bullets: Name a specific module, trading simulation, placement year, or faculty focus
Explain why that feature matters to how you learn or what you want to do
Show awareness of what makes this course different from similar ones
idealAnswer.modelAnswer: Your course has a live trading floor simulation built into second year, which is rare, and I want to learn finance by actually making decisions under pressure rather than only through case studies. I also looked at the option to specialise in corporate finance in the final year, which fits where I think I want to end up. Most courses I looked at were heavier on theory with the practical work bolted on as an afterthought, and here it felt built in from the start.

commonMistakes: Citing only league table rank
An answer that would fit any university with a finance course
Not knowing any actual course content
followUps: Which module are you most looking forward to, and why?

question: What's a book, article, or piece of financial news you've read recently, and what did you take from it?
lookingFor: Real evidence of wider reading with a genuine, digested opinion rather than a name-dropped title.

bullets: Name something specific, not just 'the Financial Times' in general
Summarise the actual argument or event accurately and briefly
Give a personal reaction or question it left you with
idealAnswer.modelAnswer: I've been reading Liar's Poker, and what struck me wasn't the trading floor drama everyone talks about but how much of it came down to information asymmetry between salespeople and clients. It made me think about how much regulation since then has actually tried to close that gap, so I've started following coverage of MiFID II to see if it worked. I don't think I have a firm view yet, but it's the kind of question I want to dig into properly at university.

commonMistakes: Naming a title with no detail on its content
Describing news without any personal reaction
Picking something clearly chosen to sound impressive rather than genuinely read
followUps: Did anything in it change your mind, or did it mostly confirm what you already thought?

question: Do you have any experience, work or otherwise, that's given you insight into banking or finance?
lookingFor: A specific, honestly-described experience with reflection on what it taught them, even if modest in scale.

bullets: Pick a real experience, even a small one, rather than inflating it
Describe what you actually did, not just the title of the programme
Reflect on a specific thing it taught you about the field
idealAnswer.modelAnswer: I did a week of work shadowing at a local branch of a retail bank, mostly sitting in on customer meetings about mortgages and small business loans. What surprised me was how much of the job was translating risk policy into a conversation a nervous first-time buyer could actually understand. It made me realise finance isn't only about spreadsheets, there's a whole layer of judgement and communication sitting on top of the numbers, which is part of why I want to study it properly rather than assume I already understand it.

commonMistakes: Exaggerating a brief or informal experience into something it wasn't
Only listing the name of the programme with no detail
No reflection on what was actually learned
followUps: What was the most surprising or confusing part of that experience?

question: Can you explain the difference between commercial banking and investment banking?
lookingFor: A clear, accurate distinction between the two core functions, showing basic fluency in industry structure.

bullets: Commercial banking: deposits, loans, everyday retail and business banking
Investment banking: raising capital, underwriting, M&A advisory, trading
Note that some banks combine both under one roof
idealAnswer.modelAnswer: Commercial banking is what most people interact with day to day, taking deposits and making loans to individuals and businesses, and it makes money mainly on the spread between what it pays savers and what it charges borrowers. Investment banking is different, it's about helping companies and governments raise capital by issuing shares or bonds, advising on mergers, and trading securities, and it earns fees rather than a lending spread. Big universal banks like JPMorgan actually do both under one roof, which is part of what makes the sector confusing from the outside.

commonMistakes: Confusing the two entirely
Only naming one side and guessing at the other
Describing investment banking as just 'trading stocks'
followUps: Which side of that split interests you more, and why?

question: What does it mean to say money has a 'time value'?
lookingFor: A correct grasp of why a sum today is worth more than the same sum later, with a real-world reason.

bullets: A given amount of money now is worth more than the same amount in the future
Explain why: it can be invested to earn a return, plus inflation erodes future value
Give a simple example to ground the idea
idealAnswer.modelAnswer: It means that a hundred pounds today is worth more than a hundred pounds in a year's time, because if I had it now I could invest it and it would grow, and because inflation will likely make that future hundred pounds buy less anyway. That's the whole reason interest rates exist, they're essentially the price of waiting for your money. It's also why loans and mortgages are structured around discounting future payments back to a present value.

commonMistakes: Confusing time value with simple inflation only
No example to demonstrate real understanding
Describing it as just 'money changes value over time' with no mechanism
followUps: How would you roughly work out what a payment of $1,000 in five years is worth today?

question: What's the difference between simple interest and compound interest?
lookingFor: Correct technical understanding with a clear worked intuition, not just a memorised formula.

bullets: Simple interest is calculated only on the original principal
Compound interest is calculated on principal plus previously earned interest
Show why compounding accelerates growth over time
idealAnswer.modelAnswer: Simple interest is calculated only on the original amount you put in, so if I invest a hundred pounds at five percent simple interest I earn five pounds every year, no more. Compound interest is calculated on the principal plus whatever interest has already been added, so that five pounds itself starts earning interest the following year too. Over a short period the difference looks small, but over decades it becomes huge, which is really the whole logic behind starting to save early.

commonMistakes: Mixing up which one grows faster
Stating the definition without any numerical example
Confusing compounding frequency with the concept itself
followUps: Why does the compounding period, monthly versus annually, matter to the final return?

question: What is the basic difference between a stock and a bond?
lookingFor: Correct grasp of ownership versus debt, plus an understanding of the risk and return trade-off.

bullets: A stock is a share of ownership in a company
A bond is a loan to a company or government that pays fixed interest
Note the difference in risk and typical return between the two
idealAnswer.modelAnswer: A stock is a small piece of ownership in a company, so if the company does well your shares can rise in value and you might get dividends, but if it does badly you can lose most of your money. A bond is really a loan, you're lending money to a company or government and they promise to pay you interest and return the principal at the end, so it's generally more predictable but with lower upside. That trade-off between the steadier bond and the riskier but potentially higher-return stock is one of the first things that got me interested in how portfolios are built.

commonMistakes: Saying both are 'the same thing, just investments'
Getting risk and return backwards
No mention of ownership versus lending as the core distinction
followUps: Why might a bond still lose value even though it pays a fixed interest rate?

question: Can you explain what happens, broadly, when a central bank raises interest rates?
lookingFor: A working understanding of monetary policy transmission, ideally tied to a real recent example.

bullets: Higher rates make borrowing more expensive, which cools spending and investment
This is typically used to bring down inflation
Mention a real-world example or trade-off, such as slower growth or mortgage costs
idealAnswer.modelAnswer: When a central bank raises rates, borrowing becomes more expensive across the economy, mortgages, credit cards, business loans, so people and companies tend to spend and invest less. That reduced demand is meant to cool inflation, which is usually why the rate rise happened in the first place. The trade-off I've been following is how the recent rate rises squeezed variable-rate mortgage holders quite hard while inflation only came down slowly, which shows the tool isn't precise or painless.

commonMistakes: Only stating that rates went up with no explanation of the mechanism
Confusing central bank rates with the returns on savings accounts alone
No connection to a real example or current event
followUps: Who tends to be hurt most by a rate rise, and who benefits?

question: What are the three main components of a company's balance sheet, and how do they relate to each other?
lookingFor: Correct recall of assets, liabilities, and equity, plus the accounting identity linking them.

bullets: Assets: what the company owns or is owed
Liabilities: what the company owes to others
Equity: the residual value belonging to owners, where assets equal liabilities plus equity
idealAnswer.modelAnswer: A balance sheet has assets, which are everything the company owns or is owed, like cash, inventory, and equipment. Then liabilities, which is everything the company owes, like loans and supplier payments. Equity is what's left over for the owners once you subtract liabilities from assets, and the whole thing has to balance, assets always equal liabilities plus equity, which is why it's called a balance sheet in the first place.

commonMistakes: Confusing the balance sheet with the income statement
Forgetting equity as the third component
Not knowing that assets must equal liabilities plus equity
followUps: How is a balance sheet different from an income statement?

question: Why is higher risk generally associated with higher potential return in investing?
lookingFor: Understanding that investors demand compensation for uncertainty, with a concrete example.

bullets: Investors need to be compensated for taking on the chance of loss
If a risky asset offered the same return as a safe one, nobody would hold the risky one
Use a concrete comparison, like government bonds versus equities
idealAnswer.modelAnswer: Investors won't accept extra risk for free, so riskier assets have to offer a higher expected return to attract anyone to hold them at all. If a risky emerging market bond paid the same yield as a safe government bond, everyone would just buy the safe one, so the risky bond has to offer more to compensate for the extra chance of default. That's why government bonds are seen as close to risk-free but low-yielding, while equities can offer much higher long-run returns alongside much bigger swings.

commonMistakes: Claiming higher risk guarantees higher return
No example to anchor the explanation
Treating risk and volatility as unrelated to return at all
followUps: Is there such a thing as a truly risk-free asset? What comes closest?

question: What is diversification, and why do investors do it?
lookingFor: A correct grasp of spreading risk across uncorrelated assets, not just 'don't put all your eggs in one basket' with nothing behind it.

bullets: Spreading investments across different assets to reduce exposure to any single one
Explain that it works best when the assets don't all move together
Give a simple example of what could go wrong without it
idealAnswer.modelAnswer: Diversification means spreading your money across different investments rather than putting it all into one company or sector, so that a problem in any single one doesn't wipe out your whole portfolio. It works best when the assets you hold don't all rise and fall together, so mixing stocks, bonds, and maybe different regions or industries smooths out the ride. I think of it like the opposite of what happened to employees who held all their retirement savings in their own company's stock and lost both their job and their savings when it collapsed.

commonMistakes: Reciting the eggs-in-one-basket phrase with no real explanation
Assuming diversification eliminates risk entirely
No mention of correlation between assets
followUps: Can you over-diversify a portfolio? What would that look like?

question: What is inflation, and who does it tend to hurt or help most?
lookingFor: A correct core definition plus real awareness of distributional effects, not just a textbook line.

bullets: Define inflation as a general rise in prices, eroding purchasing power
Identify who is hurt, such as savers and fixed-income earners
Identify who can benefit, such as borrowers with fixed-rate debt
idealAnswer.modelAnswer: Inflation is a general, sustained rise in prices across the economy, which means the same amount of money buys less over time. It tends to hurt people on fixed incomes or with cash savings sitting in low-interest accounts, because their purchasing power quietly erodes. It can actually help borrowers with fixed-rate debt, because they're paying back their loan in money that's worth less than when they borrowed it, which is one reason inflation is such a politically charged issue.

commonMistakes: Defining inflation only as 'prices going up' with no mention of purchasing power
Assuming inflation is universally bad for everyone
No distinction between winners and losers
followUps: Why might a small, steady amount of inflation actually be considered healthy for an economy?

question: What area of banking or finance are you hoping to move toward, and why?
lookingFor: A direction that's genuine and somewhat researched, while showing openness to it evolving.

bullets: Name a plausible direction, such as corporate finance, asset management, or retail banking
Explain what specifically draws them to it
Show flexibility rather than an overly rigid five-year plan
idealAnswer.modelAnswer: Right now I'm most drawn to corporate finance, the work of helping companies decide how to fund growth, whether through debt or equity, because I like that it sits close to real business strategy rather than pure trading. I know that could easily change once I've actually studied the other areas properly, and I want this course to expose me to asset management and banking too before I commit to anything. What I am sure of is that I want a role where I'm advising on decisions, not just processing them.

commonMistakes: Naming a job title with no understanding of what it actually involves
An answer entirely about salary or prestige
Sounding so fixed on one path that it seems closed-minded
followUps: What would change your mind about that direction?

question: Suppose a close friend who works at a company tells you, casually, some non-public information that would clearly affect its share price. What would you do?
lookingFor: Structured ethical reasoning showing awareness that trading on it would be insider dealing, plus practical thinking about the friendship.

bullets: Recognise that acting on the information would be insider trading and illegal, not just unwise
Reason through the discomfort of the situation rather than dismissing it instantly
Land on not trading, and consider whether to tell the friend to be more careful
idealAnswer.modelAnswer: My first reaction would be that I now know something I'm not supposed to act on, trading on it would be insider dealing regardless of how innocently I came by it, so I wouldn't buy or sell based on it, and I wouldn't pass it on to anyone else either. It would be an uncomfortable conversation, but I think I'd gently tell my friend they should be careful who they say things like that to, because it puts other people in an awkward position too. The friendship matters, but it doesn't change what the law and basic fairness to other investors require.

commonMistakes: Not recognising the situation as insider trading at all
Assuming small amounts or good intentions make it acceptable
Giving a snap answer with no reasoning shown
followUps: Would your answer change if the information came from a stranger overheard on a train?

question: What's the difference between saving and investing, and when would you choose one over the other?
lookingFor: A correct distinction based on risk, liquidity, and time horizon, with practical judgement.

bullets: Saving: low risk, easily accessible, modest or no growth
Investing: higher risk, potential for greater growth, usually a longer time horizon
Give guidance on when each makes sense, such as an emergency fund versus long-term goals
idealAnswer.modelAnswer: Saving usually means keeping money somewhere safe and accessible, like a bank account, where it's protected but grows slowly if at all. Investing means putting money into something like stocks or funds that can grow more over time but can also fall in value, and usually needs a longer time horizon to ride out the ups and downs. I'd keep an emergency fund in savings because I might need it quickly, but money I don't need for five or ten years, I'd rather have working harder through investing.

commonMistakes: Treating the two words as interchangeable
No mention of time horizon or liquidity
Giving no practical guidance on when to use each
followUps: How much of an emergency fund would you say is sensible before investing anything?

question: What is the main role of a central bank, like the Bank of England or the Federal Reserve?
lookingFor: Correct grasp of core functions: monetary policy, price stability, and financial system oversight.

bullets: Setting monetary policy, primarily through interest rates, to manage inflation
Acting as lender of last resort and overseeing financial stability
Note independence from government as a common design feature
idealAnswer.modelAnswer: A central bank's main job is managing monetary policy, mostly by setting interest rates to try to keep inflation near a target and support stable growth. It also acts as a lender of last resort, stepping in to support the banking system if there's a crisis, which is essentially what happened during the 2008 financial crisis. Most central banks, like the Bank of England, are deliberately kept somewhat independent from government so that rate decisions aren't driven by short-term political pressure.

commonMistakes: Confusing a central bank with a regular commercial bank
Only mentioning interest rates with no other function
Not knowing the difference between the central bank and the government
followUps: Why might it matter that a central bank is independent from the government?

question: In simple terms, what caused the 2008 financial crisis?
lookingFor: A reasonably accurate, structured explanation of the causal chain, not just 'banks were greedy'.

bullets: Subprime mortgage lending and risky loans bundled into complex securities
Those securities were sold widely and were more risky than their ratings suggested
When housing prices fell, defaults spread losses through the whole financial system
idealAnswer.modelAnswer: Banks in the US had been lending mortgages to borrowers who were unlikely to be able to repay them, and then bundling those mortgages into complex securities that were sold on to investors around the world, often with ratings that made them look safer than they were. When house prices started falling and defaults rose, the losses turned out to be spread through the whole financial system rather than contained, and because banks lend to each other so heavily, the fear and losses cascaded into a full crisis. It's a good example of how risk that looks diversified on paper can still be dangerously concentrated underneath.

commonMistakes: A one-line answer with no causal chain
Blaming a single actor with no systemic explanation
Confusing it with a different crisis, like the dot-com bubble
followUps: What regulatory changes came out of that crisis that you're aware of?

question: What does GDP measure, and what are some of its limitations?
lookingFor: Correct core definition plus at least one thoughtful limitation, showing critical rather than rote thinking.

bullets: GDP measures the total value of goods and services produced in a country over a period
It doesn't capture things like inequality, wellbeing, or unpaid work
It can rise even when quality of life for many people doesn't improve
idealAnswer.modelAnswer: GDP is the total value of everything a country produces in a given period, and it's the main number people use to judge how an economy is doing. But it doesn't say anything about how that output is distributed, so GDP can grow while most people's living standards stay flat if the gains concentrate at the top. It also completely misses things like unpaid care work or environmental damage, which is why I find measures like GNH or inequality-adjusted indices interesting alongside it, even if GDP is still the most-quoted headline figure.

commonMistakes: Confusing GDP with government spending or debt
Reciting the definition with no discussion of limitations
Claiming GDP directly measures happiness or wellbeing
followUps: Can you think of a country where GDP growth might not reflect improved living standards?

question: Traditional finance theory assumes investors act rationally. Can you give an example of when real investors don't?
lookingFor: Awareness that behavioral finance challenges the rational-actor model, with a specific named bias or event.

bullets: Name a specific bias, such as loss aversion, herding, or overconfidence
Explain the mechanism with a real or plausible example
Show awareness this is a genuine field of study, not just an anecdote
idealAnswer.modelAnswer: One example is loss aversion, where people feel the pain of a loss more strongly than the pleasure of an equivalent gain, which can make investors hold onto losing stocks far too long hoping to break even instead of cutting their losses rationally. You see herding too, like during the GameStop episode in 2021, where a lot of buying seemed driven by momentum and community sentiment rather than any change in the company's actual fundamentals. It's part of why I find behavioral finance more convincing as a lens than pure efficient market theory, real people don't process information as cleanly as the models assume.

commonMistakes: Vague reference to 'emotions' with no named bias or mechanism
Confusing behavioral finance with financial fraud
Not connecting the example back to the original question about rationality
followUps: Does the existence of these biases mean markets are never efficient?

question: Tell me about a time you worked in a team on something involving money or numbers, like a school investment challenge or a fundraising project. What was your role?
lookingFor: A concrete, STAR-shaped example that shows genuine involvement with numbers and honest reflection on teamwork.

bullets: Describe a specific, real project rather than a vague generality
Explain the actual role played, especially anything numerical or financial
Reflect honestly on a challenge and what was learned
idealAnswer.modelAnswer: I took part in a national stock market challenge where our team of four managed a simulated portfolio over ten weeks. I ended up being the one who tracked our positions and pushed us to set a rule for when we'd sell a losing stock, because early on we kept holding on hoping things would recover. We finished mid-table, not top, but the process of arguing through actual buy and sell decisions with real consequences taught me far more than any classroom exercise about how emotion creeps into financial decisions.

commonMistakes: A vague answer with no specific project or numbers involved
Taking full credit for a team effort
No reflection on a difficulty or lesson learned
followUps: What would you have done differently if you'd had more time or a bigger budget?

question: What factors influence how much one currency is worth relative to another?
lookingFor: A reasonable grasp of key drivers like interest rates, trade flows, and confidence, without needing full technical precision.

bullets: Interest rate differentials between countries affect capital flows
Trade balances and demand for a country's exports or imports matter
Investor confidence and political stability also play a role
idealAnswer.modelAnswer: A big factor is interest rates, if one country's rates are higher, investors are often drawn to hold that currency to earn the better return, which pushes its value up. Trade also matters, if a country exports a lot and other countries need to buy its currency to pay for those goods, demand for that currency rises. And then there's simple confidence, if investors trust a country's political and economic stability, they're more willing to hold its currency, which is part of why currencies can swing sharply around elections or political crises.

commonMistakes: Claiming exchange rates are set entirely by governments
Only naming one factor with no others
Confusing currency value with stock market performance
followUps: What effect would a weaker currency have on a country's exporters?

question: How do you manage your own money, and has that shaped your interest in finance at all?
lookingFor: Honest, concrete detail about real personal habits, connected authentically to their interest in the field.

bullets: Describe an actual habit or system, not a vague claim of being 'good with money'
Be honest, including something imperfect if relevant
Connect it to the broader interest without overstating the link
idealAnswer.modelAnswer: I started tracking every purchase in a spreadsheet after I overspent on a trip in Year 12 and had no idea where the money had actually gone. It's not sophisticated, just categories and monthly totals, but it made me genuinely curious about budgeting tools and eventually about how banks and apps build products around exactly that kind of behaviour. I wouldn't say managing my own small amount of money makes me an expert, but it's the seed of the curiosity I want to take further.

commonMistakes: A vague claim with no actual detail or habit described
Overclaiming expertise from very limited personal experience
No connection back to the interest in finance
followUps: What's one money habit you'd like to improve?

question: What is the efficient market hypothesis, and do you think it's fully true?
lookingFor: Accurate statement of the theory plus a reasoned, opinionated critique showing independent thinking.

bullets: State the core claim: prices reflect all available information, so beating the market consistently is very hard
Give a coherent view rather than dodging the question
Support the view with a concrete example or counterexample
idealAnswer.modelAnswer: The efficient market hypothesis says that share prices already reflect all available information, so it should be extremely difficult to consistently beat the market through analysis alone, since any useful information gets priced in almost immediately. I don't think it's fully true in its strongest form, because events like the dot-com bubble or the 2008 crisis suggest prices can drift quite far from anything that looks like rational value for extended periods. I lean toward the weaker version, that markets are efficient most of the time but not always, which is really the space where behavioral finance and active investing both try to operate.

commonMistakes: Only reciting the definition with no personal view
Claiming markets are always perfectly efficient with no nuance
Dismissing the theory entirely without engaging with its logic
followUps: If markets were perfectly efficient, would there be any point in studying finance at all?

subtopic: Contribution to the course and cohort
question: What do you think you'll bring to this Banking & Finance course, beyond your grades?
lookingFor: Specific, credible strengths tied to real experience, not generic self-praise.

bullets: Name a real, specific quality or experience, not just 'hard-working' or 'passionate'
Connect it to how it would actually show up in seminars or group work
Keep it modest and credible rather than overselling
idealAnswer.modelAnswer: I think I'd bring a habit of actually questioning assumptions rather than just accepting the textbook version, which came from running our school's investment challenge team and constantly having to defend our reasoning to each other. I also genuinely enjoy explaining things, I tutored younger students in economics, so in seminars I'd probably be the one trying to make sure everyone in a group is actually following the argument, not just the loudest voice. I don't think I'm the strongest mathematician in any room I walk into, but I care about getting the reasoning right, and I think that shows in how I work with others.

commonMistakes: Generic traits like 'hardworking' or 'passionate' with no evidence
Overselling with no humility or self-awareness
An answer entirely about personal gain rather than contribution to others
followUps: Can you think of a specific moment that demonstrated that quality?
